name: Research and Sources
title: Research and Sources
answer: Students must learn to judge sources because AI chatbots can produce confident summaries containing made up quotes, incorrect dates, or citations to articles that do not exist. A fluent AI answer is not the same as a true one, so schools teach students to verify every claim against real sources and to state how they used AI. The library and its librarian remain central to this work.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: This idea is about teaching students to evaluate sources and cite them properly in a world where AI tools can generate convincing but unreliable text. Chatbots may invent quotes, get dates wrong, or point to articles that were never written, and students can be fooled by how smoothly the answer reads. The problem it solves is that research skills built only on finding an answer are no longer enough, because an answer can now be produced without any real source behind it. Students need to check claims against sources that have actually been verified, such as library databases. Citation practice and a short statement of AI use are part of showing how a piece of work was really made.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, a lesson can ask students to take an AI summary and check every claim in it against a real source, such as a library database, so they see for themselves where the tool is wrong. Students also learn how to cite a source properly and how to note when and how they used an AI tool. Many schools now ask for a short statement of AI use with major assignments, which, together with the AI use level set on the assignment, gives teachers a clear picture of how the work was made. The text describes this work across kindergarten through twelfth grade without separating it into grade bands. A research unit built together with the librarian is described as one of the best defenses against AI shortcuts.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, describing what schools now ask of students and what librarians are well placed to do. The claims about chatbots producing made up quotes, incorrect dates, or citations to articles that do not exist are presented as the reason the skill matters, not as findings from a named study. No numbers or research results are stated in the supplied text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits set out in the text are that AI chat tools cannot promise sources that have been checked and can be cited, while library databases offer exactly that. The risk is that students accept a fluent answer as a true one, so verification against a real source stays a human task. The decisions that remain with people include how to design research tasks that AI cannot simply complete, which the text places with teachers working alongside librarians. Judging sources, citing them, and stating AI use are all decisions and habits that stay with the student and the teacher, not with the tool.
